intro:
**The Inner Chambers and the Universal Charter of Human Brotherhood**

Al-Ḥujurāt, "The Private Chambers," is the forty-ninth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 18 verses of late Medinan revelation. In classical Islamic scholarship, it is revered as *Sūrat al-Akhlāq* (The Chapter of Moral Etiquette) or the *Constitutional Charter of Social Ethics*. It takes its title from verse 4, which reprimands the crude desert bedouins who arrived in Madinah and began shouting loudly for the Prophet from outside *al-ḥujurāt* (the modest private living chambers of the Prophet's wives): *“Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers—most of them do not use reason.”* In eighteen masterly, intensely concentrated verses, Sūrah al-Ḥujurāt establishes the complete micro- and macro-sociology of the Islamic community: moving progressively from the sacred etiquette due to the Messenger of Allah, to the verification of media and news reports, the ethical rules of conflict resolution, the prohibition of social sins (mockery, sarcasm, spying, and backbiting), and culminating in the immortal declaration of universal human equality in verse 13: *“O humanity! Indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”*

**The Structural Fabric of Social Sanctity**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Ḥujurāt is structured as an ascending staircase of ethical maturation across five distinct movements:

1. Etiquette with Prophetic Leadership (1–5): Mandating that believers never place their own opinions ahead of Allah and His Messenger (*lā tuqaddimū bayna yaday Allāhi wa-rasūlih*), forbidding them from raising their voices above the voice of the Prophet, and warning that disrespect toward divine authority can nullify a lifetime of good deeds without one even perceiving it.

2. Epistemology and Media Verification (6–8): Delivering the foundational rule of journalism and civil intelligence: *“O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient person with information, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful”* (49:6).

3. Peace-Making and Civic Reconciliation (9–10): Establishing mandatory judicial arbitration: if two factions of believers fall into fighting, the community must intervene to make peace between them with justice and equity; if one faction aggresses against the other, the community must stand together against the oppressor until it complies with the command of God, proclaiming: *“The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your brothers”* (49:10).

4. Social Sins and the Preservation of Human Dignity (11–12): Systematically criminalizing the subtle psychological poisons that destroy communal solidarity: forbidding men and women from ridiculing or mocking one another, outlawing defamatory insults and offensive nicknames, commanding the avoidance of negative assumptions (*ẓann*), criminalizing espionage and surveillance into the private lives of others (*wa-lā tajassasū*), and delivering the terrifying, visceral condemnation of backbiting (*ghībah*): *“And do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead?”

5. Universal Human Brotherhood and True Faith (13–18): Dismantling all racial, ethnic, national, and tribal chauvinism, declaring that human diversity exists for mutual recognition (*li-taʿārafū*), not conflict, and that character (*Taqwā*) is the sole measure of human worth. The chapter closes by distinguishing between superficial verbal surrender (*Islām*) and deep, internalized faith (*Īmān*) that transforms the heart and proves itself through selfless striving in the path of God.

verses.1:
> O believers! Do not proceed ˹in any matter˺ before ˹a decree from˺ Allah and His Messenger. And fear Allah. Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**An Address That Prohibits**

The sūrah opens with a prohibition, and the prohibition is the sūrah's way of setting its tone. The address is to the believers, and the command is not to proceed in any matter before Allah and His Messenger, and the command is the sūrah's master word for everything that follows. The word for the proceeding is the word for the stepping before, and the stepping is the sūrah's image for the whole range of the conduct it corrects, from the voice that is raised too soon to the report that is acted on too soon. The sūrah is from the late Medinan period, and it comes after the conquest of Makkah, when most of Arabia had come under the rule of the Muslim polity, and the community it addresses is the community of that later moment, larger and more diverse than the community of the earlier sūrahs.
verses.2:
> O believers! Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him as you do to one another, or your deeds will become void while you are unaware

**The Incident That Produced the Verse**

The tradition gives the verse its occasion, and the occasion is the argument between Abū Bakr and ʿUmar over the delegation of an outlying tribe. The two righteous ones each favored a different individual for the honor of receiving the delegation, and the favoring turned into a quarrel in the presence of the Prophet, and the quarrel was so loud that the voice of the Prophet was drowned out by the two. The account preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, in the narration of Ibn Abī Mulaykah, states the weight of the moment in the community's own words: the two almost earned destruction when they raised their voices before the Prophet. The almost is the sūrah's way of stating how close the moment came to the edge. One of the two recommended al-Aqrabʿ ibn Ḥabīs, the man of Banū Mujāshiʿ, and the other recommended another, and the recommendation was the matter of the argument. The sūrah's verse is the revelation that came at the moment, and the coming is the sūrah's way of stating that the incident was not passed over.

**The Voice Above the Voice**

The prohibition of the verse is stated in the measure of sound, and the measure is the sūrah's way of making the relation of the community to the Prophet visible. Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, the verse commands, and the command is the sūrah's way of fixing the distance of the voice as the distance of the rank. The voice of the one who stands before the Messenger is not to be the louder voice, and the not-louder is what the verse states. The Quran states the same principle in its standing form in the sūrah of the light, where the summons of the Messenger is not to be treated as the summons of one another, "Do not treat the Messenger's summons to you ˹as lightly˺ as your summons to one another" (24:63). The two verses together fix the teaching about the voice: the voice is the measure of the relation, and the relation is what the voice either preserves or breaks.
verses.3:
> Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of Allah’s Messenger are the ones whose hearts Allah has refined for righteousness. They will have forgiveness and a great reward

**The Hearts That Are Tested**

The word the sūrah uses for the refinement of the hearts is the word for the assay, the testing of a metal for its purity, and the word is the sūrah's way of stating what has happened to the hearts of the quiet. The exegesis gives the work of the assay in its three readings: God has tested the purity of the hearts. The testing is the assay itself; God has expanded the hearts for righteousness, and the expansion is what the assay makes possible; God has purified the intentions, and the purification is the result of the assay. The three readings are the three stages of the work, and the stages are the sūrah's way of stating that the quiet is not the cause of the refinement but its sign. The Quran states the assay in its plainest form in the verse on the losses of Uḥud, where the testing is the stated purpose of the trial, "Through this, Allah tests what is within you and purifies what is in your hearts" (3:154). The sūrah's verse takes the assay and applies it to the manner, and the application is the sūrah's claim: the trial of the life and the trial of the voice are the same trial, and the quiet is the sign of the heart that has passed.
verses.4:
> Indeed, most of those who call out to you ˹O Prophet˺ from outside ˹your˺ private quarters have no understanding ˹of manners˺

**A Group Named at the Door**

The sūrah now names the group that its first section addresses, and the naming is the sūrah's way of moving from the teaching about the voice to the persons of the voice. Those who call out to you from outside the private quarters, the verse says, and the saying is the sūrah's way of stating the subject of the section in its concrete form. The word for the private quarters is the word that gives the sūrah its name, and the word is the sūrah's way of fixing the subject. The group is the group of the callers, and the callers are the ones who stand outside the door and call to the one who is within, and the standing-outside is what the verse describes.

The Book states in the same passage what the calling revealed: the callers were outside the private rooms, and the verse treats the distance they had to cross as the reason for the judgement rather than as a mistake. the commentators connect the verse to the delegations that came to Madinah from the tribes, and the sūrah's concern is that closeness to the Prophet's household is not the same as closeness to God. The word *ḥujurāt*, the private rooms, gives the sūrah its name, and it sets the limit that the sūrah's teaching of manners draws around the Messenger's family life.
verses.5:
> Had they been patient until you could come out to them, it would have certainly been better for them. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Patience That Was Not Chosen**

The verse states the alternative to the calling, and the alternative is the patience. Had they been patient until you could come out to them, the verse says, and the saying is the sūrah's way of stating what the group could have done in place of what it did. The form of the verse is the counterfactual, the patience that was not, and the counterfactual is the sūrah's way of stating the ground of the better. It would have been better for them, the verse says, and the better is the sūrah's way of fixing the value of the patience. The sūrah's point is that the calling was not the only option, and that the option that was not chosen was the better one.

The word for patience here is the same one the sūrah uses for the virtue that marks the community's dealings with the Messenger, and the Book notes the reward that stands behind it in the same verse: that God is Forgiving and Merciful. The sūrah's method in these two verses is to state the fault, state the alternative, and state the forgiveness available for both, which is why the pair reads as correction rather than condemnation. The Book's teaching about approaching the Messenger is repeated later in the same sūrah, where the believers are told that their deeds will come to nothing if they raise their voices above the Prophet's (49:2).
verses.6:
> O believers, if an evildoer brings you any news, verify ˹it˺ so you do not harm people unknowingly, becoming regretful for what you have done

**The News and Its Bearer**

The sūrah turns from the manners of the proximity to the manners of the report, and the turn is the sūrah's way of extending its subject. The verse states its injunction in its full form, and the form is the condition, the command, and the consequence, and the three together are the sūrah's way of stating the discipline in one sentence. The condition is the evildoer who brings the news, and the bearer is stated before the news, and the stating is the sūrah's way of saying that the report is not neutral. The news is carried, and the carrier is the ground of the report's weight. The command is the verification, and the verification is the sūrah's way of stating that the community is not to act on the report as it arrives.

the commentators connect the verse to the arrival of news about a tribe that had sent a delegation, where the report of a man who came back with a failure was accepted too quickly, and the sūrah corrects the whole community rather than the reporter. The Book states the same duty in the warning that follows: the community should know that the Messenger of God is among them, and that if he followed their wishes in many matters they would be in trouble (49:7). The command to verify is therefore not only about information but about the readiness to act, which is where the damage carried by news is done.
verses.7:
> And keep in mind that Allah’s Messenger is ˹still˺ in your midst. If he were to yield to you in many matters, you would surely suffer ˹the consequences˺. But Allah has endeared faith to you, making it appealing in your hearts. And He has made disbelief, rebelliousness, and disobedience detestable to you. Those are the ones rightly guided

**The Presence That Is the Ground**

The verse states the presence of the Messenger as the ground of the order that the community is to keep, and the stating is the sūrah's way of placing the community's decisions in their setting. Know that the Messenger of God is among you, the verse says, and the knowing is the sūrah's way of saying that the presence is not to be taken for granted. The exegesis gives the presence in its two forms, and the two forms are the sūrah's way of stating its range. The first form is the presence at the moment of the revelation, the Messenger standing in the midst of the community, and the standing is the presence the verse states. The second form is the presence that continues after the standing, the presence of the one who is with the believers as long as the believers are the believers. The continuation is what the Quran states in its plainest verse on the relation, when it gives the Prophet a stronger affinity to the believers than they have to themselves (33:6). The sūrah's claim, by the two forms, is that the community functions in the presence, and that the presence is the ground on which the order of the verse stands.

**The Inversion That Would Harm**

The middle clause of the verse states the inversion, and the inversion is the sūrah's way of stating what the order is not. The exegesis gives the ground of the inversion in the standing character of the Messenger: he does not speak of his own whim, and the not-speaking-of-whim is what the Quran states in its plainest form, "Nor does he speak of his own whims" (53:3).

**The Order of the Community**

the teaching about the verse, stated in its whole, is the teaching about the order of the community. The order is the order of the revelation: the Messenger receives, and the community follows, and the following is what the presence makes possible. The Quran states the obedience in its standing form in the sūrah of the exodus, when it commands the taking and the leaving, "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it. And whatever he forbids you from, leave it" (59:7), and the taking-and-leaving is the order in its practical form. And it states the consequence of the inversion in the sūrah of the believers, where the truth following the desires of the people is the corruption of the heavens and the earth, "Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens, the earth. All those in them would have certainly been corrupted" (23:71). The sūrah's verse holds the order and its two consequences together: the presence that makes the order possible, the inversion that would break it, and the works of God in the hearts that keep the community on the side of the order.
verses.8:
> ˹This is˺ a bounty and a blessing from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**The Gift Named in Its Two Words**

The verse is the second half of a sentence that began in the previous verse, and the first half named the love and the aversion that God placed in the hearts of the community, while this one names the two works in their proper name, the bounty and the blessing. The sūrah's structure here is the sūrah's way of stating that the works have a name, and that the name is the gift. The bounty is the word for the good that benefits the one who receives it. The blessing is the word for the good that exceeds the measure of what the receiver earned or expected, and the two words are the sūrah's way of stating the gift in its two directions: the direction of the benefit and the direction of the excess. The sūrah's claim, by the naming, is that the love and the aversion are not the achievements of the community, and that the not-being-achievements is what the two words state.
verses.9:
> And if two groups of believers fight each other, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight against the transgressing group until they ˹are willing to˺ submit to the rule of Allah. If they do so, then make peace between both ˹groups˺ in all fairness and act justly. Surely Allah loves those who uphold justice

**The Dispute of the Brothers**

The sūrah turns to the relations of the believers with one another, and the first relation it states is the dispute. The verse states the basic principle for dealing with a dispute between two parties of the believers, and the principle is the sūrah's way of stating that the dispute is a matter of the community's interior and not a matter of the community's exterior. The two parties are both parties of the believers. The both-being-believers is what the verse's first word fixes, for the sūrah calls the opposing groups believers even while they are fighting, and the calling is the sūrah's way of stating that the sin of the fight does not remove the faith of the fighters. The command that follows is the command of the peace-making: make peace between them, and the peace-making is the duty of the community that stands outside the two parties, and the standing-outside is what the verse assigns to the believers who are not in the fight.

**The Justice That God Loves**

The verse closes with the love of the just, and the closing is the sūrah's way of stating the ground of the peace-making. The peace between the two is to be made with justice, and the justice is the sūrah's way of stating that the peace-maker is not the party of either, and that the not-being-party is what the justice is. The Quran states the love of the fair in its standing form in the sūrah of the two-bannered, where the fair dealing with those who have not fought is the dealing that God loves, "Surely Allah loves those who are fair" (60:8). It states the standing for justice in the sūrah of the women, where the witness for God is to stand firm even against oneself and one's kin, "O believers! Stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives" (4:135). The hadith the exegesis cites states the boundary of the conduct in the dispute: the cursing of a Muslim is a sin, and the fighting of a Muslim is disbelief, and the boundary is what the verse's peace-making keeps within.
verses.10:
> The believers are but one brotherhood, so make peace between your brothers. And be mindful of Allah so you may be shown mercy

**The Brotherhood That Is the Structure**

The verse states the brotherhood, and the statement is one of the most important statements in the Quran on the structure of the Muslim community. The believers are but brothers, the verse says, and the but-brothers is the sūrah's way of stating that the brotherhood is the whole of the relation and not one of its parts. The hadith the exegesis cites states the structure in its image: the believers are like a single structure, each part supporting the other, and the supporting is the sūrah's way of saying that the brotherhood is not a sentiment but a construction. A structure whose parts support one another is a structure that stands, and a structure whose parts do not support one another falls, and the standing is what the verse's brotherhood is for. The sūrah's claim, by the verse, is that the community is a construction, and that the construction is the brotherhood, and that the brotherhood is what the sūrah's remaining verses will show to be the ground of the conduct it commands.
verses.11:
> O believers! Do not let some ˹men˺ ridicule others, they may be better than them, nor let ˹some˺ women ridicule other women, they may be better than them. Do not defame one another, nor call each other by offensive nicknames. How evil it is to act rebelliously after having faith! And whoever does not repent, it is they who are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers

**The Boasting That the Verse Removes**

The context of the sūrah gives the verse its deeper object, and the object is the boasting on the ground of the lineage. The sūrah stresses the transition from the bonds of the tribe to the bonds of the faith, and the transition is what the verse's prohibition serves. The hadith the exegesis cites carries the warning in its full form: the people who keep boasting of the ancestors who are gone, ancestors who will be nothing but the burning coals of the fire, will stand more contemptible before God than the beetle that pushes its dung before it. The pride of the age of ignorance and the pride of the lineage have been taken from the community. The person stands before God as the pious believer or as the wretched sinner, and all the children of Adam come from the dust.

The Book states the sequel in the same verse: whoever does not repent, those are the wrongdoers. The sūrah also names the source of the fault the verse is removing — the pride of the age of ignorance — and it gives its answer in a sentence the Prophet repeated in his farewell sermon: no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except by God-consciousness. The verse's argument about ridicule and nicknames therefore rests on a fact about human beings that the sūrah states in the next verse: God made them into peoples and tribes so that they might know one another, not so that any should look down on another (49:13).

**The Three Habits the Verse Outlaws**
The verse bans three things in order. Mockery, at its head, and the Book names both men and women so that the command cannot be read as a rule for one of them. Defamation, whether by word or by sign. And nicknames, which the verse associates with the state a person was in before faith: the name of rebellion after faith is evil. The jurists read the three as a single vice with three doors. A person who laughs at another's body, family or speech, or points at him, or repeats the name he does not want, has done the same thing in three ways, and the Book says the one who does not turn back from it is among the wrongdoers.
**The Word the Prophet Used**
The report in Muslim states the principle in one line: it is enough evil for a person to despise his brother Muslim. The Prophet also warned about the tongue in terms the community repeated in its books of manners, and the verse in front of us is one of the texts the scholars of that discipline worked from. They noted the detail that the person mocked is called a brother in the same faith, so that the offence is against a bond the offender shares and not only against a stranger he will never meet.
**What the Passage Does Next**
The verse after this one bans suspicion, spying and backbiting, and it gives the picture that settled the subject for the community: do not speak ill of one another behind their backs; would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? (49:12). The two verses belong together, and the sūrah has been building towards them, since it opened by telling the believers that the most honoured among them is the most mindful of God (49:13). The chapter is a school of manners, and this verse is its lesson about the smallest weapon a person carries.
verses.12:
> O believers! Avoid many suspicions, ˹for˺ indeed, some suspicions are sinful. And do not spy, nor backbite one another. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of their dead brother? You would despise that! And fear Allah. Surely Allah is ˹the˺ Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**The Definition of the Backbiting**

The verse forbids the backbiting, and the exegesis gives the backbiting its definition in the word of the Prophet. The definition is the one preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2589): the Prophet asked the community whether they knew what the backbiting was. The answer was that God and His Messenger know best. The definition followed: the backbiting is the mentioning of the brother in the manner that he does not like. When it was said that the mentioning is true, that the brother is as it is said of him, the answer was the one that fixes the sin: if what is said is in him, the one who said it has backbitten him. If it is not in him, the one who said it has slandered him.

**The Conjecture and Its Sin**

The sūrah opens this section with the conjecture, and the conjecture is the sin of the heart that the sūrah states before the sins of the tongue. Shun much conjecture, the verse commands, and the shunning is the sūrah's way of stating that the conjecture is not to be the habit of the community. The verse states the degree of the sin: some conjecture is a sin, and the some-is-a-sin is the sūrah's way of stating that the conjecture is not all one kind, and that the kind that is the sin is the kind that the heart takes for its ground.

**The Definition of the Backbiting**

And when the backbiting opens into the slander and the false accusation, the punishment is the severe one that the sūrah of the light states, the eighty lashes and the non-accepting of the testimony of the one who accuses the chaste without the four witnesses (24:4).
verses.13:
> O humanity! Indeed, We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may ˹get to˺ know one another. Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you. Allah is truly All-Knowing, All-Aware

**The Address That Leaves the Community**

The sūrah has addressed the believers in every verse before this one, and this verse leaves the community and addresses the mankind. O mankind, the verse says, and the leaving is the sūrah's way of stating that what it has been teaching the community is the teaching of the human being as such. This is among the most famous verses of the Quran, and the fame is the sūrah's way of stating that the verse carries the sūrah's whole subject in its first word.

**The Peoples and Tribes for the Knowing**

The verse states the division of the species, and the division is given its purpose in the same breath. God made the people into peoples and tribes, and the making-into is the sūrah's way of stating that the diversity is not the accident of the species but its form. The Quran states the division in its standing form in the sūrah of the family, where the community is given its laws and its way in the plurality, "If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community. His Will is to test you with what He has given ˹each of˺ you. So compete with one another in doing good" (5:48).

---

**The Only Rank**
The verse ends with the sentence that finishes the thought: *inna akramakum ʿinda Allāhi atqākum* — the most honoured of you in God's sight is the most mindful of Him, and God is All-Knowing, All-Aware. Honour has been moved out of the ledger of ancestry and into a currency no one can inherit, buy or display, and the verse closes by naming the two attributes that guarantee the accounting is exact: He knows, and He is aware of the inside of the matter. The Prophet said the same thing in plainer words, in the report preserved in the Sunan collections and the Musnad, that God has removed the pride of the days of ignorance and its boasting about fathers: all people are from Adam, and Adam was from dust.
**Where the Ranking Lands**
A genealogy-based ranking in Arabia decided marriages, blood-money, seats in a council and who was fit to lead prayers. The verse removes the whole system in one sentence and replaces it with a quality that has no social address: *taqwā*, the caution of a person who remembers God when no one is watching. The test is not who a man's grandfather was but what he does with what he knows. This is why the verse is read from the pulpit in every age, and why it was read out in the Prophet's Farewell Sermon — the chapter's address to *mankind* is not a rhetorical flourish but the frame of the whole teaching.
verses.14:
> ˹Some of˺ the nomadic Arabs say, “We believe.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “You have not believed. But say, ‘We have submitted,’ for faith has not yet entered your hearts. But if you obey Allah and His Messenger ˹wholeheartedly˺, He will not discount anything from ˹the reward of˺ your deeds. Allah is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

**The Modesty the Verse Exalts**

The correction of the word is, in the sūrah's account, the exalting of the virtue that the word carries, and the virtue is the modesty. The verse admonishes every form of the religious pretension, and the pretension is the standing of the one who has not the state in the state of the one who has it, and the standing is what the sūrah's earlier addresses have forbidden in the form of the pride. The Quran states the admonition in its standing form in the sūrah of the star, where the purification is not to be claimed by the one purified, for the one who knows the reverent is the one who purifies.

The distinction the sūrah draws in this verse became one of the schools' standing teachings about faith and submission: *islām* describes entering the religion and its practice. *īmān* names the assent that has settled in the heart, and the sūrah states that the two are not the same in the claim a person may make. The Book makes the same distinction elsewhere, where the bedouins are described as making faith a matter of the tongue while God's knowledge is of what the hearts contain (49:16). The verse does not drive the newcomers out of the community; it tells them which word to use, and points to a deeper state to reach.
verses.15:
> The ˹true˺ believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger—never doubting—and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. They are the ones true in faith

**The Definition Stated in Its Full Form**

The sūrah now gives the positive definition of the believer, and the definition is the sūrah's way of answering the correction of the previous verse. The previous verse corrected the word, and this verse states the state that the word is the word of, and the stating is the sūrah's way of completing the teaching of the section. The exegesis gives the point of the verse: after the rebuke of the ones who claim the belief without having reached it, the verse stresses the steadfast nature of the true faith and the depth of the commitment it carries, and the steadfastness-and-depth is what the definition states.

The definition the sūrah gives here is answered again later in the same sūrah, where God reminds the claimants that He has guided them to faith if they are truthful (49:17). The Book gives the same marks of belief in Sūrah al-Anfāl, where the believers are those whose hearts fear when God is mentioned and who rely on their Lord (8:2–4). The two conditions singled out in this verse — no doubt, and striving with wealth and life — are the ones the sūrah wants the newly arrived tribes to hear, because both are tested in action rather than in speech.
verses.16:
> Say, “Do you inform Allah of your faith, when Allah ˹already˺ knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.”

**The Question That Carries the Correction**

The sūrah gives the Prophet his answer to the claim of the tribe, and the answer is in the form of the question. Would you then inform God about your religion, the verse says, and the question is the sūrah's way of stating that the claim is addressed to the wrong court. The claim of the tribe was we have believed, and the sūrah's answer places the claim before the one to whom the religion is not a matter of information, and the placing is what the question does.

The Book states the same doctrine across its addresses: nothing in the heavens or the earth is hidden from God (3:5; 14:38), and it names the smallest things in His knowledge to make the point unavoidable (6:59; 31:16). The verse's question is therefore not a reprimand for informing God but for thinking that the claim needed to be reported at all, and the sūrah makes the same response when it tells the Prophet that God knows what is in the hearts (49:16). The correction returns the matter to the place it belongs: the claim may be true or false, and neither state is a matter of information for God, but of the claimant's own account.
verses.17:
> They regard their acceptance of Islam as a favour to you. Tell ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Do not regard your Islam as a favour to me. Rather, it is Allah Who has done you a favour by guiding you to the faith, if ˹indeed˺ you are faithful

**The Favor Misplaced**

The sūrah states the error of the tribe in its second form, and the error is the counting of the submission as the favor. They count it as a favor to the Prophet that they have submitted, the verse says, and the counting is the sūrah's way of stating the direction of the tribe's thought. The exegesis gives the two lines of the counting, and the two lines are the sūrah's way of stating the ground of the error. On the one line, the tribe counts the submission as the favor because it submitted without the fighting, unlike the tribes whose submission was won in the field, and the without-fighting is what the tribe takes for the merit.

The Book completes the correction in the same verse by naming the favour that actually exists: God has conferred it on them by guiding them to faith, if they are truthful. The pattern the sūrah exposes is the habit of counting obedience as charity. It recurs in the Book's addresses to those who remind others of their gifts — the word used here for the favour is the same word used when the Book tells the Prophet not to count his own giving as a favour (92:19–20). The sūrah closes by returning the whole question to the knowledge of God, who sees what His servants do.
verses.18:
> Surely Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and earth. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.”

**The Closing of the Sūrah of the Manners**

The sūrah closes with the knowledge and the seeing, and the closing is the sūrah's way of stating the ground of everything it has taught. The sūrah has been the sūrah of the manners, the manners of the voice and the calling and the conjecture and the backbiting and the derision and the claim, and the closing places the whole of the manners on the ground of the Knower and the Seer. The exegesis gives the place of the statement in the Quran: the knowledge of the unseen and the seen is stated in the Quran in its many addresses, and the range of the addresses fixes the statement as the standing ground of the Book.

The sentence is the sūrah's closing statement, and it echoes the words of its opening: God is Hearing and Knowing (49:1) and here All-Knowing and All-Seeing. The Book closes several of its addresses with the same pairing, so that the reader ends with the fact that makes every instruction in the sūrah enforceable — the unseen of the heavens and the earth is His, and nothing of what people do escapes Him (34:2; 57:4). The manners the sūrah has taught, from the voice to the report to the nickname to the claim of faith, are so gathered up in one sentence about who is watching.
